title: Ashtpadi 7, salok: the holy company
hook: the salok praises the company of the holy

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi six: one cup of tea, traced back past every hand to the Giver. Your line was every comfort a gift. Today, a new stretch of Sukhmani begins, ashtpadis seven to twelve. Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.

Think of someone who, when they walk into a room, makes it a little easier to be good. You don't feel judged around them. You just find yourself speaking more kindly, complaining less, laughing more honestly. You leave them and notice you've been a better version of yourself for an hour, without trying. Almost everyone has met at least one person like that. For six ashtpadis, Sukhmani has been talking about the Giver and the gifts. Now, in the seventh, it turns to people: the holy, and what happens to us in their company.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO MAKES GOOD EASIER.` → `NOT JUDGED, JUST BETTER.` → `NOW SUKHMANI TURNS TO PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The salok has four short lines. First: the Supreme Lord is agam, out of reach, and agaadh, unfathomable, too deep to sound. Second: whoever speaks of Him is set free. Third: listen, friend, Nanak prays. And fourth: saadh janaa kee acharaj kathaa. The story of the holy ones is wondrous. Saadh, or saadhoo, is a holy person, someone whose life has been shaped by the Name. Acharaj is wonder, the feeling of seeing something you didn't think was possible. Notice the order. The salok starts with God beyond reach, and ends with people you can actually sit beside. That's the bridge this ashtpadi builds. The One who is too deep to sound becomes nearer in the company of those who remember Him. In Sikh life this has a very concrete shape: the sangat, the congregation, sitting together in the gurdwara, singing, eating side by side in the langar. Over the next days, the ashtpadi will list, line after line, what happens in that company. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, ten things and one. Then, if He took the ten, and the mind where God tastes sweet. The banker's capital, lent, not owned. The five thieves and grace that clears the house. Jih prasaad over dinner, over the body and the home. Every comfort a gift. A week of the Giver. Now, the Giver's people.
screen: `AGAM, AGAADH: BEYOND REACH.` · `LISTEN, FRIEND, NANAK PRAYS.` · `ACHARAJ: THE WONDROUS STORY.` · `GOD FAR, THE HOLY NEAR.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of your best company. Settle. Bring to mind one person in whose presence you become a little better. A grandparent, a teacher, a friend, someone you sat beside once and never forgot. Picture their face. Remember one thing they said, or the way they listened. Notice what happens in your body as you remember them: maybe the shoulders soften, maybe the jaw unclenches. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. Breathe in their company. Breathe out whatever you don't need to carry. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi seven. Its salok calls God beyond reach, and the story of the holy ones wondrous: acharaj.
Your line: good company. Today, send a short message to the person you pictured, and tell them, simply, that you thought of them. Day four hundred sixty-two. A week, done.

screen: `DAY 462 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF THE GIVER.` → `TOMORROW: THE FACE GROWS BRIGHT.`

howItsDone: Sikhs gather as sangat, the congregation, in the gurdwara to sing and hear the Guru's word and to eat together in langar; ashtpadi seven of Sukhmani Sahib praises that holy company.

fork.setup: the salok has called God out of reach, too deep to sound. where does it point next?
options: to the wondrous story of the holy ones.
fork.reveal: saadh janaa kee acharaj kathaa: the bridge to the One beyond reach runs through the company of the holy.

original.note: Gurmukhi: acharaj, wonder, the wondrous; the salok's word for the story of the holy.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy company means hanging around religious people.
what it means: it's the company in which God, beyond reach, feels near, and we become better without trying.
what a scholar hears: ashtpadi seven's stanzas repeat 'saadh kai sang' (in the company of the holy) line after line, the way ashtpadi six repeats 'jih prasaad'.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
